newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Slubice comes to life after averting floods.
newsitem.headline: Polish Slubice comes to life after averting floods.

text.p: Bright sunshine greeted thousands of evacuees coming back to Slubice on the German border on Friday, as the Polish town began returning to normal after a victorious two-week defence against the swollen Oder River.

More than 16,000 of the 18,000 inhabitants of Slubice, across from Germany's Frankfurt and der Oder, had to flee their homes and businesses on July 27 as a seven-metre-high flood wave threatened to swamp large parts of their town.
But on Friday Slubice was almost certain to have escaped the grim fate of Polish cities further south, such as flood ravaged Klodzko, Opole, Raciborz and Wroclaw.
Dry streets rewarded the efforts of hundreds of emergency workers who had been sand-bagging sodden dikes day and night to keep the river at bay.
On Thursday a Reuter story incorrectly suggested extensive damage in Slubice, but this was not the case.

"There is nice sunshine here and we would like it to stay. People are returning with smiles on their faces, with hope, the city is returning to life," Henryk Redlicki, a member of Slubice's flood committee, told Reuters over the telephone.
He said citizens were removing sand bags from entrances to buildings and lower windows and dismantling brick walls erected in shop-windows to protect property from water.
"Not everybody has returned yet, but I expect Slubice will be back to business-as-usual on Saturday or Sunday," he said.

Redlicki said only some streets were open to vehicles as the high level of ground water posed a threat to the town's sewage system, but that the situation would improve with every inch that water subsided in the Oder.

He said that although no water broke through the dikes, high ground water had filled most of Slubice's cellars. Authorities would have to wait before pumping it out until the river returned to its normal banks.
"The water level in the Oder is easing by up to 25 cm (10 inches) a day, which should bring it down to (the safe) maximum level of 370 cm in four to five days from the present 489 cm," he said.

Redlicki added that Slubice, learning from the experience of upstream cities, had managed to prevent looting in the deserted houses and shops. "The police have sealed off every building and there were no cases of theft," he said.

The pedestrian border crossing in Slubice is expected to be opened on Monday, but local authorities said the car crossing would take longer, because Polish and German experts had to make sure bridges were safe for traffic.

In early July southwestern Poland was hit by the worst floods in centuries, which inundated a total of 6,600 sq km (2,400 sq miles) , killing 54 people and forcing tens of thousands out of their homes. The disaster caused damage of billions of dollars.
Nearly 1,700 sq km of Poland were still under water on Friday and some 30,000 people remained displaced, but the floodwaters everywhere were receding.

The retreat, however, presented the authorities with a huge clean-up problem in cities and villages which did not have Slubice's luck. Water left garbage strewn over destroyed streets and buildings as well as rotting carcasses of drowned animals, mud and swarms of insects.
